note.note:
H&P – Detailed

Consult Summary:
Adult patient (identifies as Vincent; DOB recorded as 09 May 2016—possible charting error) with 1-week history of sore throat progressing to dry cough, mild exertional dyspnea, transient fever, and intermittent headache; remote video visit—no red-flag features elicited; conservative management and sick note provided.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Sore throat × 1 week → dry, non-productive cough beginning 1–2 days later.  
• Shortness of breath: Mild, only on exertion; began ~3–4 days ago. Able to climb stairs and exercise without limitation; no rest dyspnea.  
• Wheeze and mild chest discomfort present.  
• Fever: Subjective, low-grade during first 3 days; now resolved.  
• Headache: Intermittent; currently absent.  
• Appetite: Decreased; denies weight loss.  
• Nasal/sinus: Denies congestion.  
• Hemoptysis: Denies.  
• Course: Fluctuating “better–worse”; stayed off work 2 days this week.  
• Review of systems: Denies rashes. No other systemic complaints reported.

Past Medical History:
• No chronic medical conditions reported.  
• Specifically denies asthma and history of thromboembolic disease.

Medications:
• None currently.  
Allergies: Peanut allergy (no medication allergies noted).

Social History:
• Occupation: Employed; required recent sick leave.  
• Tobacco: Non-smoker (experimented “once or twice”).  
• Alcohol / substances: Not discussed.  
• Residence: UK for >12 years; born in USA.  
• Recent travel: Limited to Europe; none exotically remote.  
• Asbestos exposure: Denies known exposure.

Family History:
• Mother: Lung cancer.  
• No family history of clotting disorders reported.

Physical Examination:
Vitals: Not recorded.  
General / ENT / Respiratory / Cardiovascular: Examination not performed (remote); patient palpates no neck lumps.

Investigations:
• None ordered or available during video consult.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Likely self-limiting upper respiratory viral infection/viral bronchitis; other considerations include COVID-19 and new-onset reactive airway disease given reported wheeze.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Acute viral URI / viral bronchitis – Sore throat → dry cough, low-grade fever, improving trend.  
2. COVID-19 infection – Same symptom set plus appetite loss; no test done.  
3. Reactive airway disease / new-onset asthma – Wheeze and exertional dyspnea; no prior history.

Issue 1 – Acute viral upper respiratory infection / viral bronchitis (most likely):
• Assessment: Symptom pattern typical for viral illness; no concerning red flags.  
Plan:  
  – Symptomatic care: Paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented) for throat discomfort/fever.  
  – Encourage adequate oral fluids and rest.  
  – Expected improvement within 4–5 days.

Issue 2 – Possible COVID-19 infection:
• Assessment: Overlapping presentation; no confirmatory testing discussed.  
Plan:  
  – Discussed need to seek medical attention if symptoms worsen or fail to improve.  
  – No formal testing arranged during consult (patient advised to re-present if concerns).

Issue 3 – Exertional dyspnea / possible reactive airway component:
• Assessment: Mild; no history of asthma; monitor.  
Plan:  
  – Safety-net advice: If dyspnea increases at rest, wheeze worsens, or chest pain escalates, attend in-person GP evaluation or emergency services.

General plan items:  
• Sick note provided for additional days off work.  
• Red-flag education: escalating breathlessness, new/persistent fever, hemoptysis, significant chest pain → immediate medical review.  
• Follow-up: Contact GP or use service again if not improving after expected period.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: Vital signs, objective physical exam findings, medication doses, vaccination/COVID-test history.  
● Conflict: DOB indicates 8-year-old, yet patient is working adult (conflict noted).  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; minor conversational overlaps; remote setting limited examination.
